name: Caribbean
subtitle: Tropical paradise meets world-class sailing
heroImageAlt: Crystal-clear turquoise waters and lush green islands in the Caribbean
shortDescription: Escape to the Caribbean, where azure waters, gentle trade winds, and island life create the perfect yacht charter experience. Whether you're seeking adventure or relaxation, the Caribbean delivers both.
longDescription:
The Caribbean is a superyacht charter dream. This region is famous for its crystal-clear turquoise waters, vibrant marine life, consistent weather, and laid-back island culture. From pristine anchorages to world-class resorts, the Caribbean offers everything a first-time charterer needs to feel comfortable and every seasoned sailor wants for adventure.

The sailing season spans year-round, though winter (Decemberâ€“April) offers the best weather and calmest seas. Spring and summer bring fewer crowds and more spontaneous adventure. The region is home to diverse islandsâ€”each with its own vibe. You might anchor off a deserted beach for the day, dine at a beachfront restaurant by sunset, or explore colonial towns and tropical rainforests.

Charter fleets range from bareboat sailing yachts to luxury motor yachts with crews, making it accessible for everyone. Most charters include provisioning services, so you'll enjoy fresh island ingredients and water sports at every stop.
whatToExpect: Calm, warm waters perfect for swimming and snorkeling
Steady trade winds ideal for sailing
Laid-back island culture and friendly locals
Excellent provisioning at every major port
World-class diving and marine life
Sunset anchorages you'll never forget

name: Virgin Islands
subtitle: Perfect anchorages, consistent sailing, island-hopping paradise
heroImageAlt: Pristine beaches and azure waters of the US Virgin Islands
shortDescription: The Virgin Islands offer some of the Caribbean's best sailing. Consistent trade winds, calm anchorages, and island towns make this ideal for first-timers and families.
longDescription:
The Virgin Islands combine easy sailing with incredible scenery. Protected waters between islands mean shorter day sailsâ€”perfect if you're new to chartering. You'll find restaurants, bars, and shops at every stop, but plenty of deserted beaches and snorkeling spots too.

Daily sailing distances are short (5â€“15 nautical miles), so you have time to relax, swim, dive, or explore each island. Anchorages are well-marked and easy to navigate. The vibe is very laid-back, and locals are used to charter boats, so you'll feel welcomed everywhere.

Best for: families, groups (easy sailing means less experience required), and anyone wanting that perfect balance of adventure and comfort.
whatToExpect: Short day sails (5â€“15 NM) between islands
Multiple excellent anchorages daily
Towns with restaurants, bars, and provisioning
World-class snorkeling and diving
Calm, protected waters most of the year
Easy navigation for all experience levels

name: British Virgin Islands
subtitle: Island-hopping paradise, perfect anchorages, and consistent sailing
heroImageAlt: Pristine white sand beaches and clear turquoise waters of the BVI
shortDescription: The BVI are a sailor's dream: 50+ islands, protected waters, consistent trade winds, and anchorages ranging from lively beach bars to remote hidden coves.
longDescription:
The British Virgin Islands are specifically designed for yacht chartering. With over 50 islands and cays, endless anchorage options, and reliable sailing conditions, it's the Caribbean's premier island-hopping destination.

Daily sailing distances are manageable (3â€“15 nautical miles), leaving plenty of time to explore, snorkel, and relax. Each island has its own personality: Virgin Gorda's dramatic rock formations, Anegada's remote beaches, Jost Van Dyke's laid-back beach bars.

The charter infrastructure is outstandingâ€”provisioning is easy, repair services are abundant, and the sailing community is welcoming. Whether you're bareboat sailing or chartering with a crew, the BVI delivers the full yacht charter experience.
whatToExpect: 50+ islands and cays to explore
Short, manageable day sails between anchorages
Protected waters ideal for all experience levels
Excellent provisioning and marina infrastructure
Pristine snorkeling and diving sites
Active sailing community and beach bars

name: Leeward Islands
subtitle: Caribbean charm, vibrant culture, and laid-back island vibes
heroImageAlt: Colorful colonial architecture and turquoise waters of the Leeward Islands
shortDescription: The Leeward Islands offer authentic Caribbean character, colonial history, and excellent sailing with a more adventurous edge.
longDescription:
The Leeward Islandsâ€”Antigua, St. Kitts, Nevis, Aruba, and their neighborsâ€”blend Caribbean beauty with Old World charm. Antigua is the sailing hub of the Eastern Caribbean, host to the legendary Antigua Sailing Week. Colonial architecture, local culture, and world-class restaurants define this entire region.

The sailing is a bit more challenging than other Caribbean destinations (stronger trade winds), making it perfect for intermediate sailors. But first-timers shouldn't be intimidatedâ€”charter companies here are excellent at working with all experience levels.

You'll experience authentic Caribbean culture: local markets, steel drum music, historic forts, and genuine island hospitality. The pace is slower, the islands are less crowded, and the character is more distinctly Caribbean.
whatToExpect: Stronger trade winds and more interesting sailing
Less crowded than mainstream Caribbean
Rich colonial history and local culture
Authentic Caribbean markets and dining
Dramatic volcanic landscapes
Excellent anchorages and protected bays

name: St. Martin & St. Barts
displayName: St. Martin & St. Barts Yacht Charter
subtitle: Twin island luxury, cosmopolitan dining, and exclusive Caribbean sailing
heroImageAlt: Colorful harbor and sailboats with crystal clear waters of St. Martin
shortDescription: St. Martin and St. Barts form a natural charter pairing just 15 miles apartâ€”cosmopolitan French culture, upscale dining, and some of the northern Caribbean's most beautiful sailing.
longDescription:
St. Martin and St. Barts are natural sailing partners. St. Martin's dual French-Dutch character creates a cosmopolitan energyâ€”excellent provisioning, world-class dining, and a sophisticated sailing scene. Just 15 miles south by sail, St. Barts is synonymous with understated luxury: pristine anchorages, the picturesque harbor of Gustavia, and beaches that rival anywhere in the Caribbean.

Most charter itineraries from this area cover both islands across a week, making it easy to experience two distinct personalities without long passages. The sailing conditions are excellent with reliable trade winds and protected waters. Nearby Anguilla and the BVI add further variety for longer trips.

What makes this pairing special is the balance: you get French sophistication, Caribbean warmth, and excellent sailing grounds in one itinerary.
whatToExpect: Cosmopolitan dining and provisioning on St. Martin
Exclusive anchorages and luxury atmosphere on St. Barts
Short 15-mile sail between the two islands
Pristine beaches and crystal-clear snorkeling waters
Consistent trade winds and reliable sailing conditions
Easy access to Anguilla and other northern Caribbean islands

name: St. Lucia
subtitle: Dramatic volcanic peaks, world-class sailing, and island charm
heroImageAlt: The iconic Pitons rising from turquoise waters of St. Lucia
shortDescription: St. Lucia's dramatic volcanic landscape, excellent sailing conditions, and vibrant island culture make it a premier destination for charterers seeking natural beauty and adventure.
longDescription:
St. Lucia is instantly recognizable by its iconic Pitonsâ€”two dramatic volcanic peaks rising directly from the sea. Beyond the stunning scenery, the island offers excellent sailing conditions, protected anchorages, and authentic Caribbean culture.

The sailing here is rewarding with good trade winds and varied terrain. You'll navigate past dramatic cliffs, anchor in sheltered bays, and explore volcanic beaches and lush rainforests. The island's infrastructure is well-developed for charter boats, with excellent provisioning and repair services.

What sets St. Lucia apart is its authenticity. The island has maintained its character while embracing tourism thoughtfully. You'll find excellent restaurants blending international and local cuisine, friendly locals, and a rhythm of life that feels genuinely Caribbean.
whatToExpect: Iconic Pitons and dramatic coastal scenery
Consistent trade winds and good sailing conditions
Multiple protected anchorages and bays
Lush rainforest and volcanic beaches
Excellent restaurants and local markets
Authentic Caribbean culture and hospitality

name: The Grenadines
subtitle: The Caribbean's finest island chainâ€”pristine, unhurried, and made for sailing
heroImageAlt: Lush volcanic islands and calm blue waters of the Grenadines chain
shortDescription: The Grenadines stretch 100 miles from St. Vincent to Grenadaâ€”a string of volcanic islands, quiet anchorages, and authentic Caribbean life that remains refreshingly uncrowded.
longDescription:
The Grenadines are what the Caribbean looked like before the cruise ships arrived. Stretching from St. Vincent in the north to Grenada in the south, this 100-mile island chain is tailor-made for sailing. Bequia, Mustique, Canouan, Union Island, Carriacou, and Petite Martinique are just a few of the stops along a classic Grenadines week itinerary.

Each island has its own personality: Bequia is the sailor's favoriteâ€”a traditional fishing island with excellent provisioning and a warm community. Mustique is where celebrities go for total privacy. Union Island has a lively harbor. Grenada anchors the southern end with its spice markets, chocolate farms, and welcoming character.

The sailing is idealâ€”manageable distances, consistent trade winds, and anchorages that feel genuinely remote. This is the Caribbean at its most authentic.
whatToExpect: Over a dozen distinct islands to explore in one itinerary
Manageable sailing distances between anchorages
Authentic Caribbean culture away from tourist crowds
Excellent provisioning on Bequia and Grenada
Pristine snorkeling and diverse marine life
A rhythm of island life that slows you down in the best way

name: Turks & Caicos
subtitle: Crystal-clear waters, pristine beaches, and exclusive island escapes
heroImageAlt: Pure white sand beaches and impossibly clear turquoise waters of Turks and Caicos
shortDescription: Turks & Caicos features some of the Caribbean's clearest waters, most pristine beaches, and a more exclusive, less-crowded sailing experience.
longDescription:
Turks & Caicos is Caribbean sailing at its most pristine. The islands are known for impossibly clear water (visibility to 200+ feet), white-powder beaches, and a more exclusive atmosphere than mainstream Caribbean destinations.

The sailing is straightforward with good trade winds and calm, clear waters. Anchorages are excellentâ€”many in remote locations where you'll feel like the only boat in the world. The islands offer few crowds and excellent natural resources: pristine reefs, abundant marine life, and untouched beaches.

The infrastructure is modern and well-developed for luxury charters, with excellent provisioning and anchorage services. This is a destination for sailors seeking pristine beauty without the crowds that come with more established charter hubs.
whatToExpect: Crystal-clear waters with excellent visibility
Pristine, uncrowded beaches and anchorages
Excellent diving and snorkeling opportunities
Modern infrastructure and provisioning services
Calm seas and reliable sailing conditions
Exclusive, peaceful island atmosphere

name: Bahamas
subtitle: Pink sand beaches, bioluminescent bays, and pure relaxation
heroImageAlt: Crystal clear turquoise waters and white sand beaches of the Bahamas
shortDescription: The Bahamas offer shallow, crystal-clear waters, stunning beaches, and a slowdown-and-relax vibe that's hard to beat.
longDescription:
The Bahamas are synonymous with yacht charter luxury and ease. Shallow, warm waters mean excellent snorkeling right from your boat. Pink sand beaches, bioluminescent bays, and friendly locals create a magical atmosphere.

The Exuma Cays are the charter hubâ€”a series of islands with protected anchorages, sandy bottoms perfect for anchoring, and everything from deserted beaches to lively beach bars. Sailing distances are short, and the waters are so clear you can see the sea floor from deck.

First-timers often choose the Bahamas because the charter experience feels effortless. You'll spend more time swimming and relaxing than worrying about navigation or sailing conditions. The lifestyle here is pure island time.
whatToExpect: Shallow, crystal-clear turquoise waters
Perfect white and pink sand beaches
Calm seas and gentle winds
Excellent anchorages with sandy bottoms
Swimming and snorkeling from your boat daily
Bioluminescent bays at night

name: Exumas
subtitle: The Bahamas at their finestâ€”365 cays, impossible water clarity, and total freedom
heroImageAlt: Turquoise shallow waters and deserted sandbars of the Exuma Cays
shortDescription: The Exuma Cays are the crown jewel of Bahamas sailingâ€”365 cays, sandbars you can anchor next to, swimming pigs, and water so clear it looks like you're floating above the sea floor.
longDescription:
The Exumas are the reason people fall in love with the Bahamas. A chain of 365 cays stretching south from Nassau, the Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park is one of the western hemisphere's premier protected sailing areas. The water is shallow, warm, and impossibly clearâ€”on calm days you can see the sandy bottom 20 feet below your keel as if you were in a swimming pool.

Highlights include the famous swimming pigs of Pig Beach, the sharks of Compass Cay, the iguanas of Allen's Cay, and the natural pools of Thunderball Grotto (where the Bond film was shot). Each cay offers something different, and the distances between stops are short enough to make multiple anchorages per day entirely possible.

This is sailing at its most carefreeâ€”throw the anchor in a sandy patch, swim off the boat, watch the sunset, repeat.
whatToExpect: 365 cays with varied anchorages and experiences
Exceptional water clarity throughout the chain
Wildlife encounters: swimming pigs, nurse sharks, iguanas
Thunderball Grotto snorkeling
Protected sailing in calm, shallow waters
Easy, low-stress navigation ideal for all levels

name: Abacos
subtitle: Northern Bahamas sailing, historic settlements, and protected cruising grounds
heroImageAlt: Historic pastel-colored settlement and calm turquoise waters of the Abacos
shortDescription: The Abacos offer the Bahamas' best sailingâ€”consistent winds, well-protected cruising grounds, charming historic settlements, and a sailing culture that runs deep.
longDescription:
The Abacos are the Bahamas' best-kept sailing secret. Located in the northern Bahamas, this boomerang-shaped chain of islands forms a protected cruising ground that sailors have treasured for decades. The Sea of Abaco is sheltered by the outer barrier cays, creating calm conditions even when the Atlantic is rough.

The historic settlements of Hope Town, New Plymouth, and Man-O-War Cay are gemsâ€”pastel-painted New England-style houses built by Loyalists who arrived after the American Revolution. Hope Town's striped lighthouse is one of the most photographed in the Bahamas. Each settlement has its own character, from the bustle of Marsh Harbour (the main provisioning hub) to the quieter anchorages further south.

The Abacos tend to attract sailors who've done the Exumas and want more: better sailing conditions, more authentic settlements, and a genuine cruising community.
whatToExpect: Protected cruising grounds with consistent winds
Historic Loyalist settlements worth exploring on foot
Excellent provisioning in Marsh Harbour
Strong local sailing community and camaraderie
Good snorkeling on the outer reef
Quieter and more authentic than the Exumas

name: Mediterranean
subtitle: Historic coastlines, world-class sailing, and timeless charm
heroImageAlt: Dramatic cliffs and azure waters of the Mediterranean
shortDescription: The Mediterranean is a sailing legend. Ancient ruins, charming villages, incredible food, and world-class anchorages make it the gold standard for yacht charters.
longDescription:
Chartering in the Mediterranean is about more than sailingâ€”it's about lifestyle. You'll anchor in coves where Caesar once sailed, dine on fresh seafood caught that morning, explore centuries-old villages, and meet locals who've lived the maritime life for generations.

The sailing varies by season and region. Summer (Juneâ€“September) offers calm seas and perfect weather. Spring and fall bring steadier winds for more dynamic sailing. Winter is for experienced sailors seeking adventure.

The Mediterranean works for all experience levels because charter companies here have perfected the experience. Bareboat is an option for confident sailors; crewed charters let you focus on relaxation while the crew handles navigation. Either way, you'll feel the romance of Mediterranean sailing.
whatToExpect: World-class cuisine at every port
Ancient history and charming villages at every stop
Dramatic coastal scenery
Diverse sailing conditions depending on region and season
Excellent provisioning and chandlery services
A lifestyle experience, not just a sailing trip

name: Greece
subtitle: 6,000 islands, ancient history, and the birthplace of sailing
heroImageAlt: Iconic whitewashed buildings and turquoise waters of the Greek islands
shortDescription: Greece is sailing's original home. With 6,000 islands spanning the Aegean and Ionian Seas, ancient ruins at every anchorage, and world-class cuisine, it remains the Mediterranean's most rewarding charter destination.
longDescription:
Greece has more coastline than almost any country on Earth, and it shows. Over 6,000 islandsâ€”from the famous Cyclades (Santorini, Mykonos, Paros) to the lush Ionians (Corfu, Kefalonia, Lefkada) to the wild Dodecanese (Rhodes, Kos, Patmos)â€”create sailing grounds diverse enough for a lifetime of exploration.

The sailing varies by region. The Ionian Sea offers protected, calm waters ideal for families and beginners. The Aegean delivers stronger meltemi winds in summer and more open passagesâ€”rewarding for intermediate and experienced sailors. The Saronic Gulf, just south of Athens, is a perfect week-long circuit with history at every stop.

What makes Greece enduringly special is the combination: whitewashed villages on volcanic clifftops, ancient ruins you can anchor beneath, food that tastes of olive oil and sea salt, and a culture of genuine warmth toward visiting sailors. This is where sailing was invented, and it shows.
whatToExpect: Island-hopping across Cycladic, Ionian, or Dodecanese sailing grounds
Ancient Greek ruins accessible directly from the water
Iconic whitewashed villages and blue-domed churches
Variable conditions from calm Ionians to breezy Aegean meltemi
Exceptional Greek cuisine and local wine at every port
A warm, welcoming culture with deep maritime roots

name: Croatia
subtitle: 1,200 islands, medieval walled cities, and the Adriatic's finest sailing
heroImageAlt: Medieval walled city of Dubrovnik rising from the Adriatic Sea
shortDescription: Croatia's Dalmatian Coast is Europe's most celebrated sailing groundâ€”1,200 islands, UNESCO heritage cities, and some of the clearest waters in the Mediterranean.
longDescription:
Croatia's Dalmatian Coast has earned its reputation as Europe's premier sailing destination. Over 1,200 islands line the coast, creating a natural labyrinth of protected channels, hidden coves, and dramatic limestone cliffs that plunge directly into turquoise water.

The sailing is excellent with reliable winds, manageable distances, and a mix of island typesâ€”from the popular hub islands with excellent restaurants and marinas to completely remote anchorages where you'll be alone. The medieval cities of Dubrovnik and Split are UNESCO World Heritage sites, and arriving by yacht makes the experience even more magical than approaching by land.

Croatia's wine is exceptional, the seafood is fresh and affordable, and the infrastructure has grown to support both bareboat and crewed charters at a high standard. Summer is busy but rewarding; spring and fall offer better sailing and fewer crowds.
whatToExpect: 1,200 islands with diverse sailing options
UNESCO heritage cities visited by sea
Dramatic limestone cliffs and hidden coves
Reliable winds and well-charted waters
Excellent local wine, seafood, and cuisine
Strong bareboat and crewed charter infrastructure

name: Balearic Islands
subtitle: Mallorca, Ibiza, Menorca, and Formenteraâ€”Spain's island sailing circuit
heroImageAlt: Dramatic limestone coastline and turquoise waters of the Balearic Islands
shortDescription: The Balearics offer four distinct islands in one sailing circuitâ€”Mallorca's dramatic mountain scenery, Ibiza's cosmopolitan energy, Menorca's unspoiled coves, and Formentera's Caribbean-like beaches.
longDescription:
The Balearic Islands sit in the western Mediterranean and form one of Europe's great sailing circuits. Each island has a completely distinct character: Mallorca is the largest, with dramatic Tramuntana Mountain scenery dropping to the sea, charming port towns, and excellent provisioning. Ibiza mixes cosmopolitan nightlife with a UNESCO-listed old town and the pristine island of Formentera just a short sail away. Menorca remains the least developedâ€”quiet coves, wild nature, and a pace of life that feels unhurried.

A week charter can comfortably cover all four islands. The sailing conditions are good with reliable summer winds and warm, clear water. The infrastructure is excellentâ€”modern marinas, world-class provisioning, and a well-established charter fleet. This is Mediterranean sailing with Spanish character: excellent food, late nights, and a genuine joie de vivre.
whatToExpect: Four distinct islands in one itinerary
Mallorca's dramatic Tramuntana mountain coastline
Ibiza's cosmopolitan dining and nightlife
Menorca's pristine, uncrowded coves
Formentera's Caribbean-quality beaches just offshore
Excellent provisioning and marina infrastructure throughout

name: Italy
subtitle: Amalfi Coast cliffs, Sardinian waters, and the world's finest cuisine by sea
heroImageAlt: Colorful villages clinging to the Amalfi Coast cliffs above the Mediterranean
shortDescription: Italy's coastline is a study in contrastsâ€”the dramatic Amalfi Coast, Sardinia's Caribbean-rivaling beaches, Sicily's ancient ruins, and the Italian Riviera's elegance. All united by exceptional food.
longDescription:
Italy offers more sailing variety than almost any Mediterranean country. The Amalfi Coast is instantly recognizableâ€”brightly painted villages clinging to vertical cliffs, the scent of lemon groves from the water, and anchorages with UNESCO views. Sardinia is the Mediterranean's best-kept secret: pristine waters, uncrowded beaches, and a wild coastline that rivals the Caribbean for beauty. Sicily adds ancient Greek temples, active volcanoes (Stromboli), and some of the best food in Europe. The Italian Riviera around Portofino is sophisticated and beautiful.

The sailing quality varies by region. The Tyrrhenian Sea between the mainland and Sardinia can be lively; the waters around Sicily require some experience. But the reward matches the effort: exceptional anchorages, extraordinary cuisine at every port, and the sense that you're sailing through one of history's great civilizations.

Italy is best experienced slowlyâ€”spend time in each place, eat well, and don't rush.
whatToExpect: Dramatically varied coastlines across different regions
Exceptional Italian cuisine and wine at every port
Iconic Amalfi Coast villages and anchorages
Sardinia's pristine, uncrowded beaches and waters
Ancient Greek and Roman ruins visible from the sea
Active volcanoes and dramatic island scenery

name: French Riviera
subtitle: Côte d'Azur glamour, Corsican wilderness, and Mediterranean sophistication
heroImageAlt: Luxury yachts anchored along the glamorous French Riviera coastline
shortDescription: The French Riviera is the Mediterranean's most glamorous sailing regionâ€”Saint-Tropez, Cannes, Monaco, and Nice on the mainland, with wild Corsica a day's sail away for those seeking contrast.
longDescription:
The French Rivieraâ€”the CÃ´te d'Azurâ€”is synonymous with Mediterranean glamour. Port towns like Saint-Tropez, Cannes, Antibes, and Nice are world-famous, and arriving by yacht is the best possible entrance. The sailing is excellent with reliable winds, beautiful anchorages, and the ÃŽles d'HyÃ¨res offering pristine protected sailing just off the coast.

For sailors wanting to escape the glitz, Corsica is a day's sail from the mainland and feels like a different worldâ€”granite mountains plunging to the sea, pristine coves, authentic Corsican culture, and far fewer crowds. Many charterers combine a few days on the Riviera with a week exploring Corsica, creating an itinerary that balances sophistication with wild adventure.

The infrastructure is outstandingâ€”provisioning is excellent, marinas are world-class, and the French approach to food means every port stop is a culinary experience.
whatToExpect: World-famous port towns: Saint-Tropez, Cannes, Antibes, Nice
Glamorous marina atmosphere and superyacht culture
Pristine ÃŽles d'HyÃ¨res for quieter, protected sailing
Wild, dramatic Corsica as a nearby contrast
Exceptional French cuisine and wine throughout
Reliable sailing winds and warm Mediterranean waters

name: Turkey
subtitle: The Blue Voyage, ancient ruins at every anchorage, and legendary Turkish hospitality
heroImageAlt: Turquoise waters and pine-forested mountains of the Turkish Riviera
shortDescription: Turkey's Aegean and Mediterranean coasts offer the Blue Voyageâ€”a legendary sailing tradition through pristine bays, ancient Greek and Roman ruins, and some of the most hospitable culture in the world.
longDescription:
Turkey's coastline is one of the Mediterranean's great undiscovered (by most) secrets. The Blue Voyageâ€”a sailing tradition dating to the 1950sâ€”follows the Turkish Aegean and Mediterranean coast through an endless succession of pristine bays, pine-forested mountains, and ancient ruins. Bodrum is the traditional starting point, with its crusader castle and vibrant sailing scene. The coast east toward GÃ¶cek, Fethiye, and Kas offers hundreds of protected anchorages and ruins accessible only by boat.

What makes Turkey extraordinary is the combination of sailing quality, cultural depth, and value. You get genuine Mediterranean sailing conditions, extraordinary history (the ruins of ancient Greek and Roman cities are everywhere), legendary Turkish hospitality, and excellent foodâ€”all at a fraction of the cost of equivalent experiences in France, Italy, or Greece.

The sailing is excellent with consistent winds, well-protected anchorages, and excellent provisioning in the major towns.
whatToExpect: Pristine bays and anchorages with virtually no crowds
Ancient Greek and Roman ruins accessible only by water
Legendary Turkish hospitality and generosity
Excellent provisioning and reasonable prices
Consistent sailing winds along the Aegean and Med coasts
Outstanding fresh seafood and Turkish cuisine

name: North America
subtitle: Tropical keys to glacial fjordsâ€”the full range of sailing in one continent
heroImageAlt: Scenic Pacific Northwest coastline with mountains and forested islands
shortDescription: North America spans the full spectrum of charter sailingâ€”from Florida's tropical waters to Alaska's glacial wilderness, with New England's historic harbors, the Pacific Northwest's dramatic coastline, and the Chesapeake's sheltered sailing in between.
longDescription:
North America is wildly underrated as a charter destination. The continent spans every climate and sailing environment: tropical Florida, the history-rich New England coast, the dramatic Pacific Northwest wilderness, the remote spectacle of Alaska, and the sheltered sailing of the Chesapeake Bay. No other region on Earth offers this range.

For North American sailors, these destinations offer world-class charter experiences without the complexity of international travel. Modern marinas, excellent provisioning, and English-speaking communities reduce friction. The sailing is no less rewarding than the Mediterranean or Caribbeanâ€”just different.

Seasonal timing matters here more than in tropical regions: summer is prime season for most areas, though Florida is year-round and Alaska is best in June through August.
whatToExpect: Full range of sailing environments from tropical to subarctic
Modern marina infrastructure and excellent provisioning
Rich maritime history across all regions
Wildlife viewing opportunities in every region
No passport required for US citizens
Seasonal conditionsâ€”summer is generally prime season

name: Florida
subtitle: Year-round tropical sailing, the iconic Florida Keys, and world-class fishing
heroImageAlt: Crystal clear turquoise waters and palm-fringed islands of the Florida Keys
shortDescription: Florida is North America's only year-round tropical charter destination. The Keys offer an island-hopping experience reminiscent of the Caribbean, while the Gulf Coast and Miami area provide their own distinct appeal.
longDescription:
Florida is the gateway to Caribbean-style sailing without leaving the US. The Florida Keysâ€”a 120-mile chain of islands stretching southwest from Key Largo to Key Westâ€”offer clear turquoise water, excellent fishing, world-class diving on the only living coral reef in the continental US, and the laid-back culture that has made Key West one of America's most beloved destinations.

Biscayne Bay and the waters off Miami offer a different experience: the backdrop of one of America's great skylines, excellent provisioning, and the vibrant energy of a world city combined with protected sailing waters. The Florida Gulf Coastâ€”from Fort Myers through the Ten Thousand Islandsâ€”provides quieter, more remote sailing with outstanding wildlife.

Florida's year-round warmth makes it unique in North American sailing. Charter season never really closes, and the water stays warm enough for swimming in most months. This is the most accessible tropical sailing experience for anyone based in the eastern United States.
whatToExpect: Year-round warm weather and tropical waters
Florida Keys island-hopping with Caribbean-quality water clarity
The only living coral reef in the continental US
World-class sportfishing alongside casual cruising
Key West's legendary culture and nightlife
Easy access and excellent charter infrastructure statewide

name: New England
subtitle: Historic harbors, lobster on the dock, and classic American sailing
heroImageAlt: Classic wooden sailboats in a historic New England harbor with lighthouse
shortDescription: New England is American sailing at its most classicâ€”centuries-old harbors, lobster shacks on working docks, dramatic coastline, and a maritime culture that shaped the nation.
longDescription:
New England sailing is steeped in history and character. Maine's rockbound coast is the crown jewelâ€”thousands of islands, historic fishing villages, and some of the most dramatic coastal scenery in North America. The water is cold (it keeps the crowds away), the lobster is extraordinary, and the culture feels genuinely old and authentic. Penobscot Bay and the waters around Mount Desert Island are exceptional sailing grounds.

Further south, Rhode Island's Narragansett Bay is the historic heart of American yachtingâ€”Newport has hosted America's Cup races and maintains a sailing culture unlike anywhere else in the country. Massachusetts' Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard, and Nantucket offer classic summer sailing with beautiful harbors, excellent provisioning, and the summer energy of iconic American resort towns.

The prime season is June through September. August is peak, with warm temperatures and reliably good sailing conditions. Late September brings foliage color to the Maine coast, creating one of the most beautiful sailing backdrops in the world.
whatToExpect: Historic harbors with centuries of maritime character
Maine's island-rich coast and rockbound scenery
Fresh New England lobster, clams, and seafood at every stop
Newport's legendary American yachting culture
Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket summer harbor scene
Fall foliage along the Maine coast in September

name: Chesapeake Bay
subtitle: America's greatest estuary, protected sailing, and maritime heritage
heroImageAlt: Classic sailboats on the broad waters of the Chesapeake Bay at sunset
shortDescription: The Chesapeake Bay is America's largest estuary and one of its finest sailing groundsâ€”200 miles of protected water, historic colonial towns, blue crab feasts, and a sailor-friendly culture that welcomes all levels.
longDescription:
The Chesapeake Bay stretches 200 miles from the Susquehanna River in Maryland to the Atlantic at Hampton Roads, Virginiaâ€”and the protected waters in between are some of the best cruising grounds in North America. With hundreds of rivers, creeks, and coves to explore, a charterer could spend weeks without repeating an anchorage.

The historic towns along the Bay are highlights in themselves: Annapolis is the sailing capital of the US East Coast, with a maritime history going back to colonial times. Oxford, St. Michaels, and Chestertown on the Eastern Shore retain their 18th-century character. Norfolk and the Virginia shore offer their own distinct charm.

The Chesapeake is famous for blue crabsâ€”eating them steamed with Old Bay seasoning at a waterfront restaurant is a quintessential Bay experience. The sailing is generally gentle, making it excellent for families and beginners while still offering enough variety to keep experienced sailors engaged.
whatToExpect: 200 miles of protected sailing with hundreds of anchorages
Historic colonial towns with authentic maritime character
Blue crab feasts at waterfront restaurants
Annapolisâ€”the sailing capital of the US East Coast
Gentle, protected sailing ideal for all experience levels
Excellent birding and wildlife throughout the estuary

name: Pacific Northwest
subtitle: Dramatic wilderness, wildlife everywhere, and one of the world's great sailing regions
heroImageAlt: Snow-capped mountains and forested islands reflected in calm Pacific Northwest waters
shortDescription: The Pacific Northwestâ€”from Puget Sound through the San Juan Islands into British Columbia's Gulf Islands and Desolation Soundâ€”is North America's most dramatic sailing ground, combining wilderness, wildlife, and world-class beauty.
longDescription:
The Pacific Northwest sailing region spans from Puget Sound in Washington State north through British Columbia to Desolation Sound, one of Canada's most beloved cruising destinations. The scenery is extraordinary: snow-capped peaks reflected in calm waters, old-growth forests dropping to the shoreline, and a wildlife density that rivals anywhere in the world.

Orca whales, humpbacks, sea otters, bald eagles, black bears, and seals are regular sailing companions. The anchorages range from the bustling marinas of the San Juan Islands to completely remote BC coves where you'll hear only the sound of the forest and sea. Desolation Soundâ€”despite the ominous nameâ€”is one of the most beautiful cruising areas in North America, with warm (for the Pacific Northwest) waters and spectacular mountain scenery.

The sailing is variableâ€”calm inland waters in the San Juans give way to tidal rapids and open coast passages in BC. This is a region that rewards sailors with some experience, though the San Juans alone offer excellent cruising for beginners. Best season is June through September.

name: Alaska
subtitle: Glaciers, humpback whales, and sailing at the edge of the world
heroImageAlt: Tidewater glacier calving into the sea with snow-capped mountains in Alaska
shortDescription: Alaska is bucket-list sailing at its most rawâ€”tidewater glaciers calving into the sea, humpback whale pods, brown bears on the shoreline, and a sense of wilderness that is genuinely overwhelming.
longDescription:
Alaska sailing is unlike anything else in North America. The Inside Passageâ€”a protected waterway stretching from British Columbia to Southeast Alaskaâ€”passes through some of the most dramatic and remote scenery on the planet. Glacier Bay National Park alone is worth the journey: a UNESCO World Heritage site where tidewater glaciers calve into the sea, and the entire landscape is still being revealed from under the ice that covered it just 250 years ago.

The wildlife is extraordinary at a different scale from anywhere else. Humpback whales feed on herring just off your bow. Brown bears fish for salmon on the riverbanks you anchor near. Sea otters wrap themselves in kelp to sleep next to your hull. Bald eagles are so common they become background.

This is expedition-level charter sailing, best done with an experienced captain. The conditions can be serious, the distances are real, and the remoteness means self-sufficiency matters. But the reward is a sailing experience that resets your sense of what's possible on the water.

Humpback whale pods feeding alongside your boat

name: Asia-Pacific
subtitle: Remote islands, exotic cultures, and world-class sailing

longDescription:
Asia-Pacific sailing is for adventurous souls. You'll explore less-trampled islands, encounter rich cultures, and sail in waters that feel genuinely remote. Thailand, Indonesia, and Australia offer excellent charter opportunities with diverse experiences.

The sailing is variableâ€”some areas are protected and easy, others require more skill. But the payoff is an authentic adventure: diving pristine reefs, anchoring in hidden lagoons, and connecting with island communities.

Charter seasons are specific to each location (monsoons matter here), so planning is crucial. But those who make the effort find it transformative.

name: Thailand
subtitle: Limestone karsts, tropical islands, and world-class sailing at remarkable value
heroImageAlt: Dramatic limestone karst islands rising from turquoise waters in Thailand
shortDescription: Thailand is Southeast Asia's premier sailing destinationâ€”dramatic limestone karsts rising from turquoise water, excellent diving, vibrant culture, and some of the best value for money in the world.
longDescription:
Thailand's sailing grounds are centered on the Andaman Sea, with Phuket as the gateway and the islands of Phang Nga Bay, the Phi Phi Islands, and the Similan Islands within easy reach. The scenery is unforgettable: enormous limestone karst formationsâ€”some rising 300 meters from the seaâ€”frame sheltered bays and hidden lagoons.

The sailing conditions are good during the dry season (Novemberâ€“April), with warm waters, reliable breezes, and extraordinary visibility underwater. The provisioning is excellent and affordable, the local cuisine is world-class, and the cultural experiencesâ€”floating markets, Buddhist temples, fishing villagesâ€”add depth that purely tropical destinations lack.

What makes Thailand exceptional as a sailing destination is the combination of dramatic scenery, excellent diving, rich culture, and value. You get luxury sailing at a fraction of Mediterranean prices, with an experience that is genuinely different from anything in the Western hemisphere.

name: Raja Ampat

shortDescription: Raja Ampat is the world's most biodiverse marine environment. Remote islands, pristine reefs, and world-class diving make it the ultimate destination for serious divers and adventure sailors.
longDescription:
Raja Ampat (Four Kings) in northwest Papua represents the pinnacle of dive tourism. The waters contain unparalleled biodiversityâ€”75% of the world's coral species and over 1,500 fish species. For divers, it's the ultimate destination. For sailors, it's one of the world's most remote and beautiful sailing areas.

The sailing here is more adventurousâ€”you need to plan carefully for weather and logistics. But those who venture here find truly pristine waters and islands where you may be the only yacht visible. The local culture remains authentic, provisioning requires planning, and the natural beauty is unmatched.

What makes Raja Ampat special is that it remains genuineâ€”not yet fully tourist-ified. The diving and snorkeling are extraordinary, and the sailing adventure is real.

name: Komodo

longDescription:
Komodo National Park is uniqueâ€”a collection of volcanic islands most famous for their native Komodo dragons. But the real appeal for sailors is the dramatic scenery, pristine sailing conditions, and access to some of Indonesia's least-explored islands.

The sailing here is excellentâ€”good winds, protected waters, and manageable distances between islands. Anchorages are pristine, often completely empty. The diving and snorkeling are world-class, with healthy reefs and abundant fish life. The local culture remains authentic, and interaction with local communities is rewarding.

What makes Komodo special is the combination of famous wildlife (the dragons), dramatic scenery, and pristine sailing. This is adventure sailing with a side of natural wonder.

The Whitsunday Islands are 74 tropical islands strung across the Coral Sea off Queensland's coast. Each island has its own character: some developed with resorts, others completely wild. The sailing is excellent with manageable distances, good wind conditions, and countless anchorage options.

The real draw is access to the Great Barrier Reefâ€”the world's largest coral reef system. Snorkeling and diving here are legendary. The islands are lush and tropical, the waters are warm and clear, and the Australian culture is welcoming. Provisioning is excellent, and the infrastructure supports both bareboat and crewed charters.

What makes the Whitsundays special is that they combine tropical island beauty with Great Barrier Reef accessâ€”an unmissable combination.

name: New Zealand
subtitle: City of Sails, Hauraki Gulf islands, and world-class Pacific sailing
heroImageAlt: Sailboats in the Hauraki Gulf with Auckland skyline and volcanic islands
shortDescription: New Zealand is the southern hemisphere's sailing capital. Auckland's Hauraki Gulf offers 50+ islands for day-sailing, while the Bay of Islands and Marlborough Sounds reward those willing to venture further.
longDescription:
New Zealand is one of the world's great sailing nationsâ€”per capita, more New Zealanders sail than almost any other nationality, and it shows in the infrastructure, culture, and quality of the sailing experience. Auckland, the City of Sails, sits at the gateway to the Hauraki Gulf with 50+ islands within easy reach.

The Hauraki Gulf Marine Park is the starting point for most chartersâ€”protected waters, diverse islands, and easy access to both urban Auckland and remote anchorages. Further north, the Bay of Islands is a sailing institution: 144 islands, excellent fishing, and a warmth in the water and culture that surprises first-time visitors. In the South Island, the Marlborough Soundsâ€”a drowned river valley systemâ€”create some of the most sheltered and dramatic sailing in the country.

New Zealand sailing combines world-class sailing culture with extraordinary sceneryâ€”volcanic islands, fjord-like sounds, and a maritime character that runs through every part of the country.

Chartering in Central and South America is an expedition. You'll explore places most tourists never reach: rainforest rivers, remote Pacific islands, and untamed coastlines. The sailing is variable, so this works best for intermediate to advanced sailors.

This isn't a relaxation charterâ€”it's an adventure that expands your worldview.

name: Belize

Belize is uniqueâ€”the only English-speaking Central American country with a Caribbean coastline. It combines Caribbean sailing beauty with jungle adventure and Mayan archaeological sites. The country has a well-established tourism infrastructure while maintaining authentic cultural character.

The sailing is excellentâ€”calm protected waters, multiple islands to explore, and access to the world's second-longest barrier reef. The Cayes (islands) range from developed tourist hubs to remote hideaways. Diving and snorkeling are world-class. The mainland offers jungle adventure, archaeological sites, and genuine rainforest experience.

What makes Belize special is that you get Caribbean sailing plus Central American adventureâ€”and everything is English-speaking and accessible.

name: Costa Rica
subtitle: Pura vida by seaâ€”wildlife-rich waters, jungle coastlines, and Pacific adventure
heroImageAlt: Lush jungle coastline and pristine Pacific waters of Costa Rica
shortDescription: Costa Rica's Pacific coast offers some of Central America's most wildlife-rich sailingâ€”dolphins, whales, sea turtles, and abundant marine life in protected waters backed by lush rainforest.
longDescription:
Costa Rica is Central America's most established ecotourism destination, and the sailing reflects that. The Pacific coastâ€”from the Nicoya Peninsula south to the Osa Peninsulaâ€”is wild, beautiful, and rich with wildlife. Dolphins ride the bow wave regularly, humpback whales migrate through in season, sea turtles nest on remote beaches, and the jungle canopy literally touches the water in many places.

The sailing is variable and requires some experienceâ€”Pacific swells and currents demand more attention than protected Caribbean sailing. But the reward is access to places few travelers ever see: remote beaches, uninhabited islands, and ecosystems that feel primordial. The Osa Peninsula and Cocos Island (for liveaboard divers) represent the wild end of the spectrum.

Costa Rica's famous pura vida cultureâ€”a philosophy of easy living and appreciationâ€”permeates every interaction. The infrastructure for charter sailing is developing but not as mature as Caribbean destinations; this suits adventurous sailors who want something real rather than polished.

name: Galápagos

longDescription:
The GalÃ¡pagos Islands are unlike anywhere else on Earth. Isolated 600 miles off Ecuador's coast, the islands have evolved unique wildlife found nowhere else: giant tortoises, flightless cormorants, marine iguanas. Darwin visited here and it shaped his theory of evolution.

Sailing here is genuinely adventurous. Conditions are variable, planning is crucial, and regulations are strict (to protect the ecosystem). But the reward is an experience that transcends sailingâ€”it's a journey to a primordial world. You'll see wildlife found nowhere else, explore volcanic landscapes, and understand why the GalÃ¡pagos inspired one of history's greatest scientific insights.

What makes the GalÃ¡pagos special is that it's not just sailingâ€”it's a transformative experience. Come here and you'll understand why conservation matters.

name: Northern Europe

Chartering in Northern Europeâ€”Norway, Sweden, Scotlandâ€”is a bucket-list adventure. Stunning fjords, midnight sun summers, and crisp air create a magical sailing environment. The sailing is well-established, with excellent infrastructure and safety records.

Summer is the prime season (Juneâ€“August), when the midnight sun creates an ethereal sailing experience. Spring and fall bring fewer crowds and more challenging sailing. Winter is for arctic adventurers.

This region suits sailors who love nature, dramatic scenery, and the cooler sporting side of sailing. Provisioning is excellent, communities are welcoming, and the sailing experience is world-class.

name: Norway
subtitle: World's most dramatic fjords, midnight sun, and sailing at the top of the world
heroImageAlt: Dramatic Norwegian fjord with sheer cliffs and calm reflective water
shortDescription: Norway's fjords are among the world's most dramatic sailing groundsâ€”sheer walls of rock rising thousands of feet from the water, waterfalls cascading into the sea, and midnight sun lighting it all in golden color.
longDescription:
Norway's fjord coast is one of the world's great sailing destinations, and it's genuinely awe-inspiring in person. The Geirangerfjord, Sognefjord (Europe's longest and deepest fjord), Hardangerfjord, and dozens of others create a labyrinthine world of sheer cliffs, hanging glaciers, and waterfalls that drop directly into the water from hundreds of meters above.

The sailing is excellent in summer (Juneâ€“August) when the midnight sun means you can sail at any hour. The winds are variableâ€”calm in the fjords, more brisk in the open coastâ€”and the distances are real. The communities along the fjords are welcoming, provisioning is good in the towns, and the infrastructure supports both cruising sailors and charter guests.

What makes Norway extraordinary is the sheer scale of the scenery. Nothing quite prepares you for your first fjord. The cliffs are bigger, the waterfalls longer, and the silence deeper than anything you can imagine. This is sailing that makes you feel very small in the best possible way.

name: Sweden

longDescription:
Sweden's Stockholm Archipelago is jaw-dropping in scale: 30,000 islands and skerries stretching from the capital far into the Baltic. You could spend months exploring and never visit the same anchorage twice. The sailing is gentleâ€”protected waters, short distances between islands, and a well-marked system of fairways and anchorages maintained by the Swedish maritime authorities.

In summer, the midnight sun means nearly continuous daylight. You can sail at 11 PM with the sun still above the horizon, casting everything in that particular Nordic gold light. The landscape is characterized by smooth granite rocks, pine and birch forests, and the clean, clear Baltic waters.

Each island has its own personality: some have small communities with guest harbors and restaurants, others are completely wild nature reserves. The Swedish outdoor cultureâ€”allemansrÃ¤tten (the right to roam public land)â€”means you can land almost anywhere and explore freely. This is sailing that rewards a slow pace: less ground covered, more appreciated.

name: Scotland
subtitle: Wild Hebrides, ancient castles on the water, and sailing at its most dramatic
heroImageAlt: Rugged Scottish coastline with ancient castle and dramatic cloudy skies
shortDescription: Scotland's west coast and Hebridean islands offer some of Europe's most dramatic sailingâ€”wild anchorages beneath ancient castles, white sand beaches backed by mountains, and a fierce, beautiful landscape unlike anywhere else.
longDescription:
Scotland's west coast is a world apart. The Hebridean islandsâ€”Inner and Outerâ€”stretch into the Atlantic in a chain of dramatic, windswept landscapes: white beaches of shell-sand (as white as the Caribbean, and considerably colder), black mountains dropping to sea lochs, ancient castles on headlands, and skies that change by the minute.

The sailing is real sailingâ€”variable winds, Atlantic swells, and tidal streams that require attention and experience. But the reward matches the challenge. Anchorages like Loch Scavaig on Skye, surrounded by the Cuillin mountains, are among the most dramatic in the world. The Corryvreckan whirlpool between Jura and Scarba is one of the largest in the world. Colonsay, Islay, Mull, and the Outer Hebrides each have distinct characters and spectacular wildness.

Whisky distilleries accessible by boat on Islay and Jura add a uniquely Scottish dimension to the sailing. The people are genuinely welcoming, the wildlifeâ€”red deer, golden eagles, basking sharks, puffinsâ€”is extraordinary, and the sense of sailing somewhere genuinely wild is unmatched in Europe.

The Indian Ocean is where yacht charter meets pure tropical fantasy. The Maldives' impossibly clear atolls, the Seychelles' granite island paradise, and Mauritius' lagoon-fringed beaches are among the world's most coveted sailing destinationsâ€”and increasingly accessible by charter.

These waters are warm year-round, marine life is extraordinary, and the setting feels unlike anywhere else. Each destination has its own character: the Maldives feels almost otherworldly, the Seychelles is a UNESCO biosphere of dramatic granite and tropical birds, and Mauritius blends French, Indian, and African cultures into something entirely its own.

Charters here tend toward the luxury endâ€”these destinations attract discerning travelersâ€”but the experience justifies every penny. This is bucket-list sailing.

name: Maldives

The Maldives sits just above the equator in the Indian Oceanâ€”a nation of 1,200 coral atolls spread across 90,000 square kilometers of turquoise ocean. Most visitors see it from a resort. Arriving by yacht lets you experience it as it was meant to be experienced: anchoring in a private atoll, snorkeling a pristine reef with no one else around, watching manta rays glide past your keel.

The sailing is gentleâ€”these are atolls, so protected waters are everywhere. The marine life is extraordinary: whale sharks, manta rays, hawksbill turtles, reef sharks, and some of the world's healthiest coral gardens. Visibility routinely exceeds 30 meters. The water temperature stays at 28â€“30Â°C year-round.

What makes the Maldives unmistakable is the waterâ€”that specific shade of turquoise that looks edited in photos but is completely real. Seeing it in person, from a yacht, is a genuinely humbling experience.

name: Seychelles
subtitle: Dramatic granite islands, UNESCO biosphere reefs, and pristine Indian Ocean sailing
heroImageAlt: Dramatic granite boulders and turquoise waters of the Seychelles

longDescription:
The Seychelles are immediately recognizable: massive rounded granite bouldersâ€”millions of years oldâ€”rise from turquoise water, framing some of the world's most dramatic beach scenes. The Seychelles archipelago spans 115 islands, but the Inner Islands around MahÃ© and Praslin are the sailing heartland.

The sailing is excellent with consistent trade winds (Mayâ€“October) and calmer conditions for the rest of the year. Distances between islands are manageable, and the anchorages range from popular to completely remote. The marine life is extraordinaryâ€”the Seychelles is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and the reefs are among the healthiest in the world. Giant tortoises roam the interior of Aldabra Atoll (one of the most pristine ecosystems on Earth).

The culture is a unique blend of African, French, British, and South Asian influencesâ€”the food is exceptional, the people are warm, and the pace of life is gentle. This is the Indian Ocean at its most civilized.

Mauritius is one of the Indian Ocean's most underrated sailing destinations. A fringing coral reef encircles most of the island, creating a natural lagoon that is warm, calm, and beautifully clear. The sailing inside the lagoon is gentle and accessible; venturing outside to the outer reef offers more challenging conditions and open-ocean encounters.

The island's culture is one of the most diverse in the worldâ€”the legacy of Dutch, French, British, African, Indian, and Chinese influences creates a cuisine and cultural experience unlike anything else in the Indian Ocean. Port Louis is a vibrant city with excellent provisioning; smaller villages around the coast maintain traditional character.

Dolphins are frequently encountered on the west coast, the snorkeling is excellent, and the sunsetsâ€”with volcanic peaks silhouetted against orange skiesâ€”are extraordinary.

name: South Pacific

longDescription:
The South Pacific is where sailors go when they want to feel genuinely far from everything. Fiji's 333 islands, French Polynesia's legendary atolls (Bora Bora, Rangiroa, the Tuamotus), and Tonga's ancient island kingdom offer sailing experiences that have no equivalent elsewhere.

The distances are realâ€”this is ocean sailingâ€”but the rewards match the effort. Lagoons of impossible clarity, coral gardens with schooling fish and sharks, Polynesian cultures that remain genuinely rooted in tradition, and skies with more stars than most people have ever seen.

This region demands capable vessels and experienced sailors, or the willingness to charter with a professional crew. It is not a beginner's destination. But for those ready, it is transformative in a way that few sailing experiences can match.

name: Fiji

heroImageAlt: Turquoise lagoon and lush tropical island in Fiji
shortDescription: Fiji is the soft coral capital of the world and the Pacific's most welcoming sailing destination. 333 islands, extraordinary diving, and the famous Fijian warmth make it impossible not to fall in love.
longDescription:
Fiji has earned its reputation as the Pacific's friendliest destination many times over. The Fijian 'bula'â€”the greeting you'll hear hundreds of timesâ€”is entirely sincere. The islands are welcoming to visiting sailors, village visits are genuine cultural exchanges, and the hospitality feels real.

The sailing is excellent. The Mamanuca and Yasawa Islands are the charter heartlandâ€”protected waters, manageable distances, and enough islands to spend weeks without revisiting anywhere. The diving is world-famous: Fiji is home to some of the most spectacular soft coral in the world, and dive sites like the Great Astrolabe Reef are legendary.

Provisioning is good in Suva and Lautoka. The sailing conditions are best from May to October (southeast trade wind season). This is South Pacific sailing with excellent infrastructureâ€”the perfect entry point to the Pacific.

name: French Polynesia
subtitle: Bora Bora, the Tuamotus, and the most iconic lagoons on Earth
heroImageAlt: Iconic overwater bungalows and turquoise lagoon of Bora Bora, French Polynesia
shortDescription: French Polynesia contains some of the most famous sailing lagoons on Earth. Bora Bora, the Tuamotu atolls, and Moorea offer extraordinary beauty, world-class diving, and the feeling of being at the end of the world.
longDescription:
French Polynesia is the Pacific at its most legendary. The 118 islands and atolls span an area the size of Europe, and within that expanse are some of the world's most iconic sailing destinations: Bora Bora with its shark-infested but extraordinarily clear lagoon, the Tuamotu atolls (Fakarava, Rangiroa) with drift dives through passes teeming with sharks and rays, Moorea with its volcanic silhouette rising from the ocean.

The sailing here is for experienced sailors or those chartering with crew. Passes into Tuamotu atolls require timing and experienceâ€”the currents are strong and the consequences of a mistake are real. But inside the lagoons, the sailing is gentle and the diving is world-class.

French influence means provisioning is excellent by Pacific standards (real baguettes, good wine, fresh produce). The combination of French sophistication and Polynesian warmth creates an atmosphere unlike anywhere else. This is the Pacific's most complete sailing destination.

Tuamotu drift dives through shark-filled passes
Excellent provisioning by Pacific standards (French influence)
Skilled navigation required for atoll passes

The experience of being genuinely far from the rest of the world

name: Tonga
subtitle: Humpback whales, pristine coral reefs, and the Pacific's last Polynesian kingdom
heroImageAlt: Humpback whale breaching with tropical island and turquoise water in Tonga
shortDescription: Tonga is the Pacific's best-kept secretâ€”an ancient Polynesian kingdom where you can swim with humpback whales, explore pristine reefs, and experience a traditional culture that has resisted outside influence for centuries.
longDescription:
Tonga is the only Pacific island nation never colonized by a foreign power, and that independence shows in its culture. The 170-island archipelago is spread across three groupsâ€”Tongatapu in the south, Ha'apai in the middle, and Vava'u in the northâ€”each with distinct character.

Vava'u is the sailing heartland: a naturally sheltered harbor surrounded by 50+ islands, described by sailors who've visited as one of the world's perfect sailing grounds. The distances are short, the anchorages are protected, and the snorkeling and diving are pristine.

But Tonga's most extraordinary experience is unique in the world: from July to October, humpback whales migrate to Tongan waters to breed and calve. With the right permit and a respectful approach, you can slip into the water alongside a 40-ton humpback and her calf. It is one of the most profound wildlife encounters on the planet, and it is legal only in Tonga.
whatToExpect: Swim with humpback whales (Julyâ€“October)â€”legal only in Tonga
Perfect natural harbor in Vava'u with 50+ islands
Short, manageable sailing distances between anchorages
Pristine reefs and exceptional snorkeling and diving
Authentic Polynesian culture largely unchanged by outside influence
Significant night-sky visibility far from light pollution
